narrative: The model estimated a 77% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, and because that is a high failure risk, your law school application was denied. The decision was driven most strongly by your third-year class-rank decile. You are in the lowest decile (1), while accepted students average about 5.8; this was the single largest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. The second most influential factor was your LSAT score. At 36 it is slightly below the accepted-student average of about 37.2, but in this prediction its effect leaned toward passing rather than failing. The third factor was your family-income bracket. Being from a middle-income family was associated with a push toward failure; among accepted students, middle income is less common than upper-middle income (about 34.8% versus 45.4%). Thus, the very low third-year rank and the family-income signal outweighed the LSAT’s favorable effect and produced the high failure estimate. To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record, especially evidence of improved performance in advanced coursework, and consider retaking the LSAT if you can raise the score. Ask admissions for feedback, document any circumstances affecting your grades, and consider applying after showing a stronger recent record or completing a preparatory program.
